title: How Drug Courts Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with guest producer Tristan) explain drug courts: specialized, treatment-focused criminal courts that began in Miami-Dade County, Florida in the late 1980s and have spread to more than 3,000 in the US. Covers eligibility, coercive structure (deferred charges or guilty pleas tied to graduation), fast treatment, judges acting as social-worker-like figures, sanctions like flash incarceration, the 12 to 24 month timeline, veteran and family services, research claims on recidivism, and criticisms from the Drug Policy Alliance and a Pacific Standard article about abstinence-based courts that ban methadone maintenance. The episode opens with a tour announcement (Salt Lake City and Phoenix dates) and ends with listener mail from Ken in Lancaster, Pennsylvania about North Korea and the DMZ.

entities.name: Commission on Combating Drug Addiction and the Opioid Crisis

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Josh, speaking as a tour announcement with Chuck, announces 2018 tour dates in Salt Lake City (October 23) and Phoenix (October) and says tickets will be posted on the venue websites.

segments.title: Opening banter and drug court introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Tristan's shaved mustache and a hypothetical arrest, then introduce drug courts as a way to treat addicted offenders rather than simply jail them.

segments.title: Origins in Miami-Dade County
segments.summary: The hosts describe the late 1980s crack epidemic and Miami-Dade judges creating what is described as the first drug court. They mention defense attorney David Scott Marcus, who was assigned to drug court under Judge Stanley Goldstein and later recovered and became an advocate. The model spread across the US to more than 3,000 courts.

segments.title: How drug courts are entered
segments.summary: Referral can come from a defense attorney, prosecutor, or arresting officer. The process is non-adversarial. Defendants may have charges deferred pending graduation or plead guilty with dismissal or expungement on completion. Treatment starts within days of arrest.

segments.title: Judges, supervision, and the coercion model
segments.summary: Judges get to know participants, test them frequently, and reduce testing as they prove clean. Failure can bring short jail stays called flash incarceration, with eventual removal to criminal court. Programs run about 12 to 24 months, and some shorter emergency programs exist for opioid cases. Judges are expected to act partly like social workers.

segments.title: Services for veterans, families, and participants
segments.summary: Drug courts connect participants with services such as help for domestic violence victims, veterans and PTSD care, child welfare navigation, and practical help getting benefits and treatment. The hosts argue this support is valuable for people who lack the ambition or resources to start themselves.

segments.title: Judicial style and graduation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the ideal judge as supportive but stern, with respect and graduations celebrated in court with other participants present. They contrast this with typical criminal court and make a joke about traffic court.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break before the research discussion.

segments.title: Research outcomes and recidivism
segments.summary: Studies cited report lower recidivism, reduced crime, saved money, better family reunification, and lower felony rearrest in Escambia County, Florida. Jail and prison data show high rates of substance abuse among inmates. Hosts caution that results reflect completers and may be cherry-picked.

segments.title: Criticisms: Drug Policy Alliance, methadone bans, and abstinence courts
segments.summary: The Drug Policy Alliance argues drug courts are still user busting and favors decriminalization. A Pacific Standard article reports that about half of drug courts ban methadone maintenance, which the medical community considers best practice for opioid addiction, raising overdose risk after release. Hosts note some courts allow it and that the data may be cherry-picked.

segments.title: Listener mail: North Korea DMZ
segments.summary: Listener Ken from Lancaster, Pennsylvania writes about visiting the DMZ, flagpole rivalry, and South Korean perspectives on reunification. The hosts recap the 1976 axe attack and the Mass Games.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts give social media handles, email address, and website, and sign off.
